questions.explanation: Few categories with many choices in each.

questions.prompt: On a planogram, "facings" means:
choices: Units of a product visible across the shelf front
questions.explanation: Facings show how many units appear side by side.

questions.prompt: A $60 item is marked down to $45. The markdown percent is:
questions.explanation: The $15 markdown divided by the $60 original price is 25%.

modules.title: Customer service process: inquiries, complaints, CRM, and follow-through
modules.summary: Answer inquiries and explain policies accessibly, resolve complaints within authority, escalate and document, use CRM records responsibly, measure satisfaction, and deliver the brand promise.

sections.heading: Inquiries and policy explanations
paragraphs: Most customer contacts are questions, not complaints. Answer with accurate information, in plain language, and confirm the customer understood. When explaining a policy the customer dislikes, give the reason briefly, then focus on what you can do: "Opened software cannot be returned because it can be copied. I can help you install it or contact the publisher's support line now."

Accessible communication meets customers where they are: speak clearly and face the customer for people who lip-read, offer written or large-print information, welcome service animals, accept relay calls, and use plain words. Cultural differences affect eye contact, personal space, directness, and how people express dissatisfaction, so watch and adapt rather than assume. Unspoken needs show up in context: a customer comparing two car seats while holding a toddler may need help with installation and time, not a faster pitch.

sections.heading: Resolve complaints step by step
steps: Hear: let the customer explain fully without interrupting.
Empathize: show you understand the impact ("Missing the delivery before your daughter's party must have been stressful").
Apologize sincerely for the experience, even before fault is known.
Resolve: offer a remedy within your authority, or explain exactly who will decide and when.
Diagnose and document: record the facts, remedy, and cause so the problem can be fixed for others.
paragraphs: Empowerment means employees can offer remedies, such as a refund up to $50 or a free replacement, without asking a manager. Escalate when the remedy exceeds your authority, the customer asks for a supervisor, safety or legal issues arise, or the conversation becomes abusive. When escalating, brief the next person so the customer does not repeat the story. Follow up after the fix. A well-handled problem can leave a customer more loyal than one who never had a problem.

example.scenario: A fictional furniture store delivered a table with a scratched top. The customer calls angry. The associate may offer up to a 15% credit or arrange a replacement.
example.solution: The associate listens, apologizes, and paraphrases the problem. They offer two options within authority: a replacement delivered on the next available date, or a 15% credit if the customer keeps the table. The customer wants the replacement plus compensation for taking another day off work, which exceeds authority, so the associate escalates to the manager with a summary, tells the customer the manager will call by 3 p.m., and records the call. The next day the associate checks that the call happened.

sections.heading: CRM records, privacy, and measurement
paragraphs: Customer relationship management (CRM) software stores contact information, purchase history, service cases, and preferences, so anyone helping the customer sees the history. Good records are accurate, factual, and professional, because customers can often request their data. Permissions limit who can see sensitive fields such as payment details. Collect only what the business needs, honor opt-outs, and never look up records out of curiosity.

Common service measures include customer satisfaction (CSAT) surveys, first-contact resolution rate, average response time, and Net Promoter Score (NPS). NPS asks how likely a customer is to recommend the business on a 0 to 10 scale. Scores of 9 or 10 are promoters; 0 to 6 are detractors. NPS equals the percent of promoters minus the percent of detractors.

example.scenario: 200 customers answer the NPS question: 110 give 9 or 10, 50 give 7 or 8, and 40 give 0 to 6.
example.solution: Promoters: 110 / 200 = 55%. Detractors: 40 / 200 = 20%. NPS = 55 - 20 = 35. The 50 passives count in the total but not in either group.

sections.heading: Selling and the brand promise
paragraphs: A brand promise is what customers expect every time, such as "fast and friendly" or "expert advice." Service delivers it or breaks it. Selling in a service role means discovering needs with questions, recommending what truly fits, demonstrating value, answering objections honestly, and closing by asking for the decision. Recommending an add-on that solves a real problem is service; pushing one that does not is not.

Emotional intelligence underlies all of it: staying calm under pressure, reading the customer's mood, and adjusting tone. Ethical choices include never promising what the company cannot deliver and treating every customer by the same standards.

practice.task: A gym member wants to cancel because of a job loss. Policy requires 30 days' notice and allows a 3-month freeze for $5 a month. Write the associate's response, including empathy, the policy explanation, options, documentation, and follow-up.
practice.answer: Sample: "I'm sorry about your job. Thank you for telling me. Cancellation takes 30 days' notice, so your last charge would be next month. Another option is a freeze for up to three months at $5 a month, which keeps your rate if you want to return. Which would you prefer?" The associate records the reason, the choice, and dates in the CRM, confirms by email, and if the member freezes, sets a reminder to check in before the freeze ends. The response explains the policy without pressure and offers a real choice.

Passing an issue to someone with more authority or expertise.
Percent of promoters minus percent of detractors on a 0 to 10 recommendation scale.
The share of issues solved during the customer's first contact.
The experience a brand commits to deliver every time.

questions.explanation: 60% promoters minus 15% detractors equals 45.

questions.explanation: Escalation is for issues beyond the associate's authority or skill.

questions.explanation: Permissions restrict who can see sensitive data.

questions.explanation: Hearing the whole problem guides the right response.

choices: Giving the reason briefly and focusing on what you can do

questions.explanation: Reasons plus options keep the customer's goodwill.

modules.title: Hospitality operations: guests, revenue, controls, and events
modules.summary: Serve guests through peak demand and recovery, manage guarantees, cash, and card payments, calculate occupancy, ADR, RevPAR, and food cost, and plan event budgets and staffing.

sections.heading: The industry and its sectors
paragraphs: Hospitality includes lodging (hotels, resorts, short-term rentals), food and beverage (restaurants, catering, bars), travel and tourism (airlines, cruise lines, attractions), recreation, and meetings and events. Demand for leisure travel is sensitive to the economy: in recessions, travelers cut trips, trade down to cheaper options, and book closer to the travel date. Business travel follows corporate budgets.

Organizations include the American Hotel and Lodging Association, the National Restaurant Association, Meeting Professionals International, and the Events Industry Council. Careers range from front desk agent and server to revenue manager, sales manager, executive chef, event planner, and general manager. Information sources include industry benchmark data, guest reviews, booking data, and trade publications. Current trends include mobile check-in and digital keys, contactless payment, sustainability programs that reduce food and linen waste, and travelers combining business and leisure trips.

sections.heading: Measure lodging and food performance

rows: Room revenue / rooms available, or occupancy x ADR
Cost of food sold / food sales

paragraphs: RevPAR combines occupancy and rate, so it shows whether a discount that filled rooms actually raised revenue. Revenue management adjusts prices by demand, raising rates for high-demand dates and offering packages or discounts for slow ones.

example.scenario: A 120-room hotel averages 60 rooms sold at $160 on weeknights. A proposed $130 rate is expected to sell 80 rooms. Which earns more?
example.solution: Current RevPAR: 60 x 160 / 120 = $80. Proposed: 80 x 130 / 120 = $86.67. The lower rate raises room revenue from $9,600 to $10,400 a night. Check that variable costs for 20 more rooms, such as housekeeping and amenities, do not exceed the $800 gain.

sections.heading: Guests, peak demand, guarantees, and recovery
paragraphs: Accurate guest orders begin with repeating the order back, noting allergies and special requests, and checking before delivery. Accessible service under the ADA includes accessible rooms and routes, service animals, and willingness to adapt. Peak demand, such as a Sunday checkout rush or a Friday dinner, is managed through reservations, staggered staff schedules, cross-training, express options, and setting honest wait times.

For catered events, the client gives a guarantee, the final attendance number, usually 48 to 72 hours before the event. The client pays for the guarantee or actual attendance, whichever is higher. Kitchens often prepare a small overset, such as 3% to 5% above the guarantee. Service recovery means fixing a guest's problem quickly and generously enough to restore goodwill: apologize, fix it, add a gesture when appropriate, and follow up.

sections.heading: Cash and card controls
paragraphs: Cash controls include assigning each cashier a separate drawer, counting banks at the start and end of shifts, requiring manager approval for voids and comps, using blind drops (deposits counted later by someone else), and two-person counts. Card payments require authorization at the time of sale. Businesses that accept cards must follow the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), which means never writing down or storing full card numbers and security codes, using secure terminals, and limiting access. Chip and contactless payments reduce fraud. A chargeback occurs when a customer disputes a charge, and the business must provide records such as a signed folio.

sections.heading: Products, security, selling, and events
paragraphs: Hospitality products combine tangible parts (the room, the meal) and service. Location (place) heavily affects value. Guest motives include rest, celebration, business needs, adventure, and status. Security includes key card control, never announcing room numbers aloud, protecting guest data, and practiced emergency plans. Selling includes upselling a room upgrade when it fits the guest's purpose and suggestive selling in restaurants.

An event budget lists revenue (registrations, sponsorships) and expenses (venue, food, audiovisual, staffing, insurance) with a contingency of around 10%. Staffing alternatives include in-house staff, temporary agency staff, contracted vendors, and volunteers, each with different costs, training needs, and reliability. Measure satisfaction with short post-event surveys, repeat bookings, and online reviews.

practice.task: A banquet's guarantee is 150 guests at $42 per person. Actual attendance is 141. (a) What is the food charge? (b) If attendance had been 158, what would the charge be? (c) The hotel prepares a 4% overset. How many meals does it prepare?
practice.answer: (a) The client pays for the guarantee: 150 x 42 = $6,300. (b) Actual exceeds the guarantee, so 158 x 42 = $6,636. (c) 150 x 1.04 = 156 meals.

terms.definition: The percentage of available rooms sold.
Average daily rate: room revenue divided by rooms sold.
Revenue per available room: room revenue divided by rooms available.
The final attendance number a client commits to pay for at a catered event.

modules.title: Sports and entertainment management: revenue, promotion, rights, and impact
modules.summary: Industry structure and revenue streams, fan motives and sponsorship, ticket pricing and distribution, publicity documents and game-day scripts, contracts and risk, and economic impact.

sections.heading: Industry structure and fans
paragraphs: Sports and entertainment includes professional, college, high school, youth, and recreational sports, plus concerts, theater, film, gaming and esports, and theme parks. Revenue comes from tickets, media rights, sponsorships, merchandise and licensing, concessions, parking, and premium seating. The core product, the game or show, is unpredictable, so marketers sell the whole experience: atmosphere, food, entertainment between plays, and social time.

Fans attend for entertainment, escape, social connection, family time, and identity with a team. Highly identified fans attend through losing seasons; casual fans respond to promotions and star players. Sponsorship gives a company association with the event in exchange for money or goods. Activation is what the sponsor does with the rights, such as a branded fan zone, and measures include audience reached, leads collected, and sales.

sections.heading: Pricing, tickets, and distribution
paragraphs: Ticket pricing uses tiers by seat location, variable pricing by opponent or date set in advance, and dynamic pricing that changes with demand. Season tickets and group packages build a base of committed fans. Premium seating and suites earn high margins from businesses. A ticket campaign combines an offer (such as a family four-pack with hot dogs), a deadline, a channel, and a way to track sales.

Distribution covers how fans access the product: the venue, ticketing platforms and the resale market, broadcast and streaming, radio, and social media highlights. Advertising media include local TV and radio, digital and social ads, outdoor signs, and direct mail to past ticket buyers, which can be targeted by zip code and tracked with codes.

sections.heading: Publicity and promotional production
paragraphs: A press release starts with "For Immediate Release" (or an embargo date), a headline, a dateline (city and date), and a lead paragraph answering who, what, when, where, and why. Body paragraphs add details and a quote from an official. It ends with a short boilerplate about the organization, contact information, and ### to mark the end. Newsletters keep season-ticket holders informed. Event programs list rosters, schedules, and sponsor ads.

A game-day script, or run of show, lists every moment with times: gates open, warm-ups, anthem, starting lineups, timeout promotions, halftime show, sponsor announcements, and post-game. Each line names the person responsible, the announcer's exact words, music, and video cues. Logos, tickets, and signage must follow brand standards and licensing rules. Celebrity appearances need a contract covering fee, schedule, travel, security, and approved activities.

example.scenario: Write the first lines of a press release for a fictional minor-league team's new sensory-friendly game.
example.solution: "FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE. Riverton Otters Host First Sensory-Friendly Game. RIVERTON, Md. (April 2, 2027) The Riverton Otters will host the league's first sensory-friendly game on May 15 at 1 p.m. at Harbor Field, with lowered music volume, no fireworks, and a quiet room staffed by trained volunteers, so that fans with sensory sensitivities can enjoy baseball with their families." A quote, details on tickets, the boilerplate, and a media contact follow.

sections.heading: Agents, governing bodies, rights, contracts, and risk
paragraphs: Agents negotiate contracts and endorsements for athletes and entertainers, owe them a fiduciary duty, and in major leagues must be certified by the players' association. Governing bodies set rules and eligibility: leagues, the NCAA and other college associations, state high school associations, and international federations. College athletes have been able to earn money from their name, image, and likeness (NIL) since 2021, under evolving rules.

Rights that can be sold include naming rights, broadcast rights, and licensing rights for merchandise. Contracts must state the parties, obligations, payment, term, and what happens on breach. Barter trades goods or services instead of cash, such as tickets for radio advertising. Insurance includes general liability, event cancellation, and coverage for property and participants. A risk assessment lists hazards (weather, crowd crush, injury), their likelihood and impact, and controls. Event readiness checks cover staffing, security, medical services, signage, and backup plans.

sections.heading: Economic impact
paragraphs: Economic impact estimates how much new money an event brings into a community. Count only spending by visitors from outside the area, since local residents would likely have spent that money locally anyway. Direct spending times a multiplier estimates total impact as the money circulates through local businesses. Multipliers vary by study, so state the assumption.

practice.task: A weekend youth soccer tournament draws 8,000 visitors from outside the county who spend an average of $120 each on lodging, food, and shopping, and 3,000 local spectators who spend $40 each. Using a multiplier of 1.6, estimate the economic impact and explain which spending you excluded.
practice.answer: Direct new spending: 8,000 x 120 = $960,000. Total impact: 960,000 x 1.6 = $1,536,000. The local spectators' $120,000 is excluded because residents would likely have spent it in the county anyway. State the multiplier as an assumption and note that the estimate depends on survey accuracy.

Ticket prices that change with demand in real time.

modules.title: The consultative sale: needs, demonstration, objections, and close
modules.summary: Research the product and buyer, discover needs with questions, demonstrate features as benefits, handle interruptions and objections, close appropriately, and rehearse an interactive pitch.

sections.heading: Prepare: product and customer
paragraphs: Know the product completely: features, how they work, limits, price, warranty, and how it compares with alternatives, including competitors' strengths. List evidence for each claim, such as test results, reviews, or a live demonstration. Research the buyer's situation if it is given: industry, size, current solution, and likely concerns.

Translate features into benefits with the FAB method: the feature (what it is), the advantage (what it does), and the benefit (what that means for this buyer). "The tablet has a 12-hour battery (feature), so it lasts a full shift (advantage), which means your servers never lose an order mid-shift (benefit)."

sections.heading: The selling sequence
steps: Approach: greet the buyer, introduce yourself, and set a friendly, professional tone.

Discover needs: ask open questions before presenting. A useful sequence is situation ("How do you take orders now?"), problem ("Where do mistakes happen?"), implication ("What does a wrong order cost you?"), and need-payoff ("How would it help if orders went straight to the kitchen?").
Present and demonstrate: show only the features that meet the needs you heard, and let the buyer handle the product when possible.
Handle objections: listen fully, acknowledge, ask a question to understand, and respond with facts.
Close: ask for a decision or an appropriate next step.
Follow up: confirm details, delivery, and satisfaction.
paragraphs: Closing techniques include the trial close ("How does that fit your kitchen?"), the alternative choice ("Would the 10-unit or 15-unit package work better?"), the summary close (restating the benefits the buyer agreed with), and the direct request. Honest urgency, such as a real promotion end date, is fine; invented urgency is not.

sections.heading: Handle interruptions and objections
paragraphs: In an interactive presentation, the buyer may interrupt at any time. Treat each question as a buying signal. Answer it directly, connect it to a need, and return to your plan without losing your place. Prepare by listing the ten most likely questions and objections and rehearsing short answers.

Common objections concern price, need, timing, the product, or the company. The feel-felt-found response acknowledges the feeling ("I understand how you feel"), shows others shared it ("other owners felt the same"), and shares what they found ("they found the order accuracy paid for the tablets in four months"). Use real evidence, not invented testimonials. If the objection is valid, admit it and show how the overall value still fits, or recommend a better alternative.

example.scenario: Fictional product: a restaurant ordering tablet. The buyer interrupts: "This costs $3,000 more than our paper tickets."
example.solution: Acknowledge and explore: "That is a real cost. Can I ask how many orders a week need to be remade?" Buyer: "Maybe 25, about $15 each." Respond with their numbers: "That is about $375 a week, or $19,500 a year. If the tablets cut remakes by even half, they would pay for themselves in about four months." Then close a step: "Would a two-week trial in one section help you see the difference?"

sections.heading: Setup, team roles, and backup
paragraphs: Plan the physical setup: where the product sits, what the buyer can touch, and how visuals are displayed. Check technology limits in the event rules, such as whether internet or electrical outlets are provided, and have a backup such as printed visuals or an offline video. For teams, assign roles (opener, demonstrator, objection handler, closer), plan smooth handoffs, and make sure every member can answer any question.
Review the rating sheet and rehearse a full pitch for a product unrelated to your competition product. Time each section and practice with a partner who interrupts unpredictably.

practice.task: Fictional product: a $40 smart water bottle that reminds the owner to drink and tracks intake in an app. Buyer: a gym manager considering selling it at the front desk. Write two discovery questions, one FAB statement, a response to "Our members won't pay $40 for a water bottle," and a close.
practice.answer: Questions: "What do members buy most at the front desk now?" and "What do members ask staff about hydration or recovery?" FAB: "The bottle tracks intake automatically, so members see their progress without logging it, which gives your trainers data to coach with." Objection: "That's a fair concern. Would it help to stock a small test quantity of 12 and see the sell-through over a month, alongside the $15 basic bottle you carry now? Members who already pay for training are often the ones who buy tracking tools." Close: "Shall we start with 12 units and a counter display, and review sales together on the 30th?"

Feature, advantage, benefit: a method for turning product facts into buyer value.
A question that checks the buyer's readiness without asking for the final decision.
A buyer's concern or reason for hesitating.

modules.title: Social media campaign workshop: research, content, budget, and metrics
modules.summary: Choose platforms from audience research, build a content plan and three connected ads, budget and schedule distribution, calculate campaign metrics, and present forecasts honestly.

sections.heading: Set the goal and research the audience
paragraphs: Start with a business objective, then a campaign goal that serves it. "Increase weekday sales 15% in six weeks" is a business objective; "get 200 people to redeem a weekday offer" is a measurable campaign goal. Avoid goals that only count likes unless awareness is truly the objective.

Build one or two audience personas from real evidence: age range, location, interests, problems, where they spend time online, and what would make them act. Use platform audience data from reliable surveys, the business's own customer data, and short interviews. Choose platforms where the audience is active and the content format fits the product. One platform done well usually beats four done poorly.
This workshop uses a fictional neighborhood bakery launching a Saturday baking class. It is unrelated to the competition topics, so students build their own campaigns.

sections.heading: Build the content plan and three connected ads
paragraphs: Content pillars are the three or four themes the account returns to, such as behind-the-scenes, tips, customer stories, and offers. A content calendar sets dates, formats, captions, and who produces each post. Mix original content with reused content, such as customer photos shared with permission and credit.

Connected ads share a visual style, a message, and a sequence. A common sequence moves the audience from awareness to consideration to action, with each ad doing one job. Captions open with a hook, give one key detail, and end with one call to action. Make content accessible: captions on every video, alt text for images, readable contrast, and hashtags written in camel case (#SaturdayBakeClass) so screen readers say them correctly.

rows: 15-second video of dough being shaped, with captions
"Ever wanted to make bread that actually rises?" Learn more
Carousel showing the class steps and the instructor
"In two hours, you'll bake a loaf and take it home." See class details
Image of finished loaves with a limited-seat offer
"Only 12 seats each Saturday. First class 20% off with code BAKE20." Book now

sections.heading: Budget, schedule, and distribute
paragraphs: Distribution channels include organic posts, paid ads, partnerships with local creators (who must disclose the partnership), email, and in-store signs with a QR code. Search optimization matters on social platforms too: use the words people search, such as "baking class near me," in captions and profiles.

Allocate a limited budget to the ad that does the hardest job, usually the action ad aimed at people who already engaged. Schedule posts when the audience is active, and plan enough frequency to be remembered without repeating the same post too often. Build in a test: run two versions of one ad and shift budget to the better performer.

sections.heading: Measure honestly

rows: Engagements / reach (state which base you use)

paragraphs: A forecast is a projection based on assumptions, such as industry-average click rates. Observed results are what actually happened. Label forecasts clearly, list the assumptions, and never present projected numbers as real results. After launch, compare observed results with the forecast and explain the adjustments you made.

example.scenario: The bakery spends $500 on ads. They deliver 50,000 impressions and 1,000 clicks, leading to 40 class bookings at $30 each.
example.solution: Each ad dollar returned $2.40 in revenue. Whether that is profitable depends on the class's costs; if ingredients and staff cost $15 per student, profit after ads is 1,200 - 600 - 500 = $100.

practice.task: Forecast a campaign: $300 budget, an assumed $8 CPM, an assumed 1.5% CTR, and an assumed 5% conversion rate. Estimate impressions, clicks, and conversions, then write one sentence that labels the forecast honestly.
practice.answer: Impressions: 300 / 8 x 1,000 = 37,500. Clicks: 37,500 x 1.5% = 562 (about 560). Conversions: 562 x 5% = about 28. Sentence: "These are projections based on assumed rates of an $8 CPM, 1.5% click-through, and 5% conversion; actual results will be measured weekly and the plan adjusted."

A research-based profile representing a target audience segment.
Clicks divided by impressions.
Revenue generated by ads divided by the amount spent on them.
A projected result based on stated assumptions, not an observed outcome.

modules.title: From reporting file to published story
modules.summary: Plan interviews, verify sources, apply media law and ethics, write leads, structure stories, attribute quotes, and finish with captions, headlines, and style.

sections.heading: Story types and news judgment
paragraphs: News judgment decides which stories matter. Common news values are timeliness, proximity, impact (how many people are affected and how much), prominence of the people involved, conflict, novelty, and human interest. Story types include hard news (events, reported quickly and objectively), features (people, trends, and places, often with a narrative lead), profiles, editorials and opinion columns (clearly labeled), reviews, sports, and investigative stories that uncover what someone wants hidden.

Media include print newspapers and magazines, broadcast, online outlets, newsletters, and podcasts. Each platform changes length and form: a print story, a 60-second broadcast script, a social post, and an online story with links and embedded video can all come from one reporting file.

sections.heading: Build a reporting file
steps: Background research: read earlier coverage, documents, and data before interviewing.
Source list: people directly involved, experts, and people affected, with contact details and how each is connected to the story.
Interview plan: open questions ("How did the shortage affect your team?"), follow-ups, and questions that check facts you already have.

Interview notes: date, time, place, exact quotes marked as quotes, and paraphrase marked separately. Ask permission before recording; Maryland generally requires the consent of everyone in a private conversation.
Verification log: each key fact, how it was confirmed, and by which source. Confirm names, titles, spellings, and numbers. Use documents and a second independent source for important claims.
Open questions: facts still unconfirmed, which do not go in the story until confirmed.
paragraphs: Evaluate sources by how they know what they claim (firsthand or secondhand), their possible interests, and their record of accuracy. A press release is a source with a purpose, not independent confirmation. Check images with reverse image searches and check social posts with the original account.

sections.heading: Law and ethics
paragraphs: Libel is a published false statement of fact that identifies a person and harms their reputation. Public officials and public figures must also prove actual malice, meaning the publisher knew the statement was false or recklessly disregarded the truth, under New York Times v. Sullivan (1964). Private persons usually need to show only negligence. Truth is a complete defense, and honest opinion based on disclosed facts is protected. Invasion of privacy includes intrusion, public disclosure of private facts, false light, and using someone's name or likeness for commercial purposes without consent.

For student media, Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) protected student expression that does not substantially disrupt school, and Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier (1988) allowed schools to restrict school-sponsored publications for legitimate educational reasons. Maryland's 2016 New Voices law gives student journalists added protection in public schools. Copyright protects others' photos, video, and writing; fair use may allow limited use for news and commentary, judged by four factors: purpose, nature of the work, amount used, and market effect.

The Society of Professional Journalists Code of Ethics has four principles: seek truth and report it, minimize harm, act independently, and be accountable and transparent. Promise confidentiality only when necessary and with an editor's approval, because you must keep it. Separate news from opinion, correct errors openly, and avoid conflicts of interest such as covering a club you lead.

sections.heading: Leads, structure, quotes, and style
paragraphs: A summary lead gives the most important who, what, when, where, why, and how in about 30 words or fewer. A delayed or anecdotal lead opens with a scene or person, then a nut graf explains why the story matters. The inverted pyramid puts the most important information first so editors can cut from the bottom. Features often use chronological or narrative structure.

A direct quote uses the speaker's exact words in quotation marks. A partial quote quotes a key phrase. A paraphrase restates in your words without quotation marks but still needs attribution. Use "said" for attribution in most cases; it is neutral. Attribute opinions and disputed facts, not common knowledge.

AP style, widely used in news writing, spells out numbers one through nine and uses figures for 10 and above, always uses figures for ages and percentages, abbreviates months with dates only for Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., and Dec., and capitalizes formal titles only before a name. Captions identify people left to right and describe the photo in present tense. Headlines use present tense, active verbs, and no unnecessary articles.

example.scenario: Facts: The school board voted 5 to 2 on Tuesday night to start high school classes at 8:30 a.m. instead of 7:25 a.m. next fall, citing research on teen sleep. Buses will cost an extra $1.2 million a year. Write a summary lead and headline.
example.solution: Lead: "County high schools will start classes an hour later next fall after the school board voted 5-2 Tuesday to move the first bell to 8:30 a.m., a change expected to add $1.2 million a year in bus costs." Headline: "Board moves high school start to 8:30 a.m." The lead has the who, what, when, and cost, and the headline uses a present-tense active verb.

practice.task: Edit this paragraph for AP style, attribution, and accuracy: "Principal Jones said the new policy, which was approved on Monday, September 8, will impact 47% of the twelve hundred students. Students are angry about it."
practice.answer: Sample: "The new policy, approved Monday, will affect 47% of the school's 1,200 students, Principal [first name] Jones said." Changes: use "Sept. 8" if a date is needed (not both day and date), "affect" instead of "impact," figures for 1,200, the principal's full name on first reference, and the unsupported claim "Students are angry" is removed unless attributed to specific students quoted in the story.

A paragraph explaining why a feature story matters, usually after an anecdotal lead.
Knowing falsity or reckless disregard for the truth, required for libel of public figures.
Identifying the source of information or a quotation.
A record of how each key fact in a story was confirmed.

modules.title: Broadcast newsroom: rundowns, scripts, and segment production
modules.summary: Select stories, build a rundown, write two-column anchor scripts timed to the second, plan interviews and B-roll, document the process, and present a segment as a team.

sections.heading: Choose stories and build the rundown
paragraphs: A newscast's producer chooses stories using news values (timeliness, proximity, impact, prominence, conflict, human interest) plus what the audience can see and hear. A strong broadcast story has visuals and sound, not just facts. Check each story's sources as carefully as in print.

The rundown is the newscast's plan. Each row lists the order, a one- or two-word slug that names the story, who reads it, the format, and its running time. Formats include a reader (anchor reads with no video), VO (voice-over: anchor reads over video), SOT (sound on tape: a clip of someone speaking), VO/SOT (video then a sound bite), and PKG (a reporter's packaged story with narration, sound bites, and a stand-up).

sections.heading: Write for the ear
paragraphs: Broadcast copy is written to be heard once. Use short sentences, one idea each, in active voice and present or present perfect tense ("The bakery reopens today"). Put attribution first ("Police say..."). Round numbers and spell out what the anchor should say: "about one-point-two million dollars." Write phonetic spellings for hard names. Avoid quotation marks and abbreviations the anchor might stumble on.
Most anchors read about 150 words per minute, or about 3 words per second. A 20-second reader is about 60 words. Time scripts by reading them aloud with a stopwatch.

Scripts often use a two-column format: video instructions on the left (camera shots, graphics, lower-third names, clip in and out times) and the audio on the right (what the anchor reads and the sound bite's first and last words, called the in-cue and out-cue).

example.scenario: Write a 20-second VO for a fictional story: a local bakery closed by a kitchen fire in June reopens today with a new oven and ten new jobs.
example.solution: VIDEO: Exterior of bakery; customers in line; baker pulling bread from new oven. AUDIO: "A Main Street favorite is back in business. Riverside Bakery reopens this morning, five months after a kitchen fire closed its doors. The owners installed a new oven and hired ten more workers. Customers lined up before sunrise for the first loaves." That is about 50 words, roughly 17 to 20 seconds when read naturally.

sections.heading: Interviews, B-roll, and production
paragraphs: Plan each interview for usable sound bites: ask open questions that invite short, vivid answers, and ask the subject to say their name and title spelled out on camera. Frame interviewees slightly off-center, looking toward the reporter, with the camera at eye level. Record in a quiet place and use a lavalier or handheld microphone close to the speaker.

B-roll is supporting video that covers narration: wide, medium, and close shots of the people and places in the story, each held 8 to 10 seconds. Natural sound (nat sound), such as an oven door closing, makes stories feel real. A stand-up is the reporter speaking on camera at the scene, often as a bridge in the middle of a package. Lower-third graphics identify speakers. Captions make the segment accessible, and credits list everyone who contributed and any licensed material.

sections.heading: Document the process and present as a team
paragraphs: Keep a production log: story pitches and why each was chosen or dropped, the verification log, script drafts with edits and reasons, equipment and software used, and problems solved. This record lets the team explain editorial choices and shows the work is original.

For a segment showcase, assign clear roles (producer, anchors, reporter, editor), rehearse handoffs, test playback on the event's equipment or a backup device, and prepare for judges' questions about why stories were chosen, how facts were checked, and what the team would change. Confirm length limits, file format, and other requirements in the current event guide.

practice.task: You have a 2:00 newscast. Stories available: a school play opening (has rehearsal video), a 3% county tax rate change (no video, but documents), a student who built a prosthetic hand for a classmate (interviews and video), and a lost dog found (photo only). Build a rundown with slugs, formats, and times that total 2:00, and explain your lead story choice.
practice.answer: Sample: 1. Open, both anchors, 0:10. 2. Prosthetic hand, PKG, 0:50. 3. Tax rate, reader with full-screen graphic of the old and new rates, 0:25. 4. School play, VO, 0:20. 5. Dog found, reader with photo, 0:10. 6. Close, 0:05. Total 2:00. The prosthetic hand story leads because it has strong human interest, local impact, and the best video and sound; the tax story is important but works as a short reader with a clear graphic.

A story format with anchor voice-over followed by a sound bite.
Supporting video shown while narration or an anchor's voice plays.
A complete reporter story with narration, sound bites, and often a stand-up.

modules.title: Video production workflow: plan, shoot, record sound, edit, and export
modules.summary: Script and storyboard a short video, frame and light shots, record clean audio, edit with pacing, add captions and credits, export correctly, and document permissions.

sections.heading: Preproduction
paragraphs: Most video problems are solved before the camera rolls. Start with the audience, the message, and the required length. Write a script or outline, then a storyboard: a sequence of simple sketches showing each shot with notes on dialogue, sound, and duration. Turn it into a shot list grouped by location so you film efficiently, and a schedule with people, places, equipment, and backup dates.

Get signed releases from everyone who appears on camera (a parent signs for minors) and permission for private locations. Plan the sound: will you use a voice-over, interviews, music, or natural sound?

sections.heading: Shots, framing, and camera settings

rows: Face or detail; emotion and emphasis
A small detail such as hands on a keyboard

paragraphs: Use the rule of thirds, leave headroom above heads, and give lead room in the direction a person looks or moves. The 180-degree rule keeps the camera on one side of an imaginary line between two people so their screen directions stay consistent. Use a tripod or stabilizer, and shoot extra footage before and after each action for editing.

Choose a frame rate and keep it consistent: 24 frames per second looks like film, 30 is common for video, and 60 allows smooth slow motion. A shutter speed about double the frame rate (1/50 for 24 or 25 fps, 1/60 for 30 fps) gives natural motion blur. Keep ISO low to avoid noise, and set white balance so white looks white under the current light.

sections.heading: Light and sound
paragraphs: Three-point lighting uses a key light (main light, to one side of the camera), a fill light (softer, on the other side, to reduce shadows), and a back light (behind the subject, to separate them from the background). A window can serve as a key light; a white poster board can bounce light as fill. Avoid placing the subject in front of a bright window.

Viewers forgive imperfect video more than bad sound. Use an external microphone close to the speaker: a lavalier clips to clothing, a shotgun mic points at the subject from just outside the frame, and a handheld suits interviews in noisy places. Wear headphones while recording. Set levels so voices peak around -12 to -6 dBFS; sound that hits 0 clips and distorts permanently. Record 30 seconds of room tone, the quiet sound of the space, to smooth edits.

example.scenario: Common faults and fixes: (a) the interview audio echoes; (b) the subject's face is dark; (c) the footage looks orange; (d) the speaker's voice is distorted on loud words.
example.solution: (a) Move to a room with soft furnishings, move the mic closer, or hang blankets. (b) Turn the subject toward the window or add a key light; do not shoot with a bright window behind them. (c) Set white balance for the light source or adjust it in editing. (d) Audio clipped above 0 dBFS; lower the gain and rerecord, since clipping cannot be fully repaired.

sections.heading: Edit, caption, and export
steps: Organize footage into folders by scene and rename clips.
Assemble a rough cut in story order, focusing on structure, not polish.
Refine the fine cut: trim pauses, vary shot sizes, and use cutaways (B-roll) to hide jump cuts.
Use J-cuts (audio of the next shot starts early) and L-cuts (audio continues into the next shot) for natural transitions. Use simple cuts most of the time; flashy transitions distract.
Mix sound: dialogue clear and consistent, music lower under speech, no sudden jumps in volume.
Color-correct so shots match, then add titles, lower thirds, captions, and credits.
Export using the required settings, often an MP4 file with H.264 video at 1920 x 1080 and the same frame rate you shot. Watch the whole export before submitting.
paragraphs: Pacing matches the mood: quick cuts build energy, longer shots allow reflection. Captions should be accurate, synced, and readable, and they are essential for viewers who are deaf or hard of hearing and for people watching with the sound off.

sections.heading: Permissions, sources, and production records
paragraphs: Use only music, footage, images, and fonts you created or have permission to use. "Royalty-free" means no per-use fee, not free of a license. Creative Commons licenses state conditions: BY requires credit, SA requires sharing under the same license, NC bans commercial use, and ND bans changes. Some events ban previously published video clips entirely, so check the guide.

Keep a production record: the script and storyboard versions, shot list, release forms, a source log for every asset, the equipment and software used, and notes on problems and fixes. Judges often ask how you made specific choices, and the record lets you answer precisely.

practice.task: Plan a 45-second video showing how a fictional student-run coffee cart prepares for its morning rush. Write a six-shot list (shot type, subject, duration), name the microphone you would use for one interview line, and give the export settings.
practice.answer: Sample shot list: 1. Wide: cart in the hallway at 7 a.m., 5 s. 2. Medium: two students setting out cups, 6 s. 3. Close-up: espresso pouring, 4 s. 4. Medium interview: manager explaining the rush, 12 s. 5. Over-the-shoulder: student taking an order, 8 s. 6. Wide: line of customers, ending on the cart sign, 10 s. Total 45 s. Use a lavalier mic on the manager for clean interview sound. Export as MP4 (H.264), 1920 x 1080, at the frame rate used to shoot, then watch the full file and confirm captions and credits.

terms.definition: A sequence of sketches showing each planned shot.
An organized list of every shot needed, often grouped by location.
Keeping the camera on one side of an imaginary line between subjects to preserve screen direction.
A setup using key, fill, and back lights.
Distortion caused when audio exceeds the maximum recording level.
An edit where the next shot's audio begins before its video.

questions.prompt: Which light is the main light source in three-point lighting?
questions.explanation: The key light is the primary, brightest light.

questions.prompt: Audio peaks should generally stay around:
questions.explanation: This leaves headroom and avoids clipping.

questions.prompt: Crossing the 180-degree line causes:
choices: Characters to appear to switch screen directions
questions.explanation: The viewer loses track of where people are facing.

questions.prompt: A Creative Commons BY-NC license requires:
questions.explanation: BY requires attribution and NC prohibits commercial use.

questions.prompt: Which shot best establishes a story's location?
questions.explanation: A wide shot shows the setting and context.

modules.title: Public service announcements: research, message, and originality
modules.summary: Research a public issue, define one audience and one behavior, write a timed script with a clear call to action, follow originality rules, and explain the process in a showcase.

sections.heading: Research the issue and choose one behavior
paragraphs: A public service announcement (PSA) aims to change knowledge, attitudes, or behavior for the public good, not to sell a product. Effective PSAs focus on one audience and one action. "Teens" and "be safer" are too broad; "high school drivers" and "put your phone in the glove box before starting the car" are specific.

Use credible sources: government agencies, peer-reviewed research, and established nonprofits. Record each fact with its source and date in a fact-check log, and use current statistics. A single strong, verified fact is more persuasive than many weak ones. This lesson's examples use distracted driving, which is not the competition topic, so students research and design their own PSA.

sections.heading: Design the message
paragraphs: State a learning goal: after watching, the viewer should know or do one thing. Choose an appeal: emotional stories create connection; facts and demonstrations build understanding; humor can make a message memorable but must not undercut a serious subject. Fear appeals work only when paired with a clear, easy action the viewer can take.
The call to action names exactly what to do: "Turn on Do Not Disturb While Driving tonight." Close with it on screen and in audio.

sections.heading: Script and storyboard to the time limit
paragraphs: Check the current event guide for the maximum length and any required elements. At about 2.5 words per second for natural narration, a 30-second PSA holds about 75 spoken words, with room for pauses and visuals. Storyboard every shot with its duration and add them up. Time the edit and trim until it fits with a small margin.

example.scenario: Write a 30-second PSA script for high school drivers about phone use.
steps: 0:00-0:05: Close-up of a phone buzzing on a car seat. Sound: notification chime. No narration.
0:05-0:15: Driver glances down; cut to the road ahead going blurry. Narration: "Reading a text takes your eyes off the road for about five seconds."
0:15-0:22: Wide shot of the same car parked; driver puts the phone in the glove box. Narration: "At 55 miles per hour, that's the length of a football field, driving blind."
0:22-0:30: Text on screen with narration: "Put your phone away before you start the car." Logo and source line.
example.solution: About 40 spoken words fill 30 seconds with room for visuals. The statistic is attributed on screen to its source and verified in the fact-check log. Every shot is original footage with signed releases.

sections.heading: Originality and the showcase
paragraphs: PSA events usually require original work. Read the guide's rules on previously published video clips, music, and images; some guides ban them entirely regardless of license. Use your own footage and either original music or music the rules allow, and keep releases for everyone on camera.

In a live showcase, explain the research findings and why you chose the audience and behavior, the script and visual decisions, the techniques, equipment, and software used, and your sources. Bring the fact-check log and production notes, and be ready to say what you would change with more time.

practice.task: Choose an unrelated public issue such as sun protection or bike helmet use. Write a one-sentence audience, a one-sentence learning goal, a specific call to action, and one verified fact with its source and date.
practice.answer: A strong answer names a specific audience (for example, middle school cyclists who ride to school), a single learning goal (they will know that a properly fitted helmet greatly reduces the risk of serious head injury), a concrete action ("Do the two-finger fit check before every ride"), and one statistic copied exactly from a government or medical source with the publication date. Vague audiences, multiple goals, or unsourced numbers do not meet the standard.

terms.definition: A message created to inform the public or change behavior for the common good.
The specific action the PSA asks viewers to take.
A record of each fact used with its source and verification.
The persuasive approach a message uses, such as emotion, logic, or humor.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest PSA call to action?
choices: Put your phone in the glove box before starting the car
questions.explanation: It names one specific, doable action.

questions.prompt: About how many spoken words fit in a 30-second PSA with room for visuals?
questions.explanation: At roughly 2.5 words per second, 75 is the upper limit; fewer leaves room for visuals.

questions.prompt: A fear appeal works best when it:
choices: Includes a clear action the viewer can take
questions.explanation: Without an achievable action, fear leads viewers to tune out.

questions.prompt: A PSA guide bans previously published clips. A licensed stock clip is:
choices: Not allowed if it was previously published
questions.explanation: The guide's rule applies regardless of licensing.

questions.prompt: Which source is most credible for a health statistic?
questions.explanation: Government agencies publish data with stated methods.

modules.title: Animation foundations: principles, timing, tools, and production
modules.summary: Apply the principles of animation, plan timing with keyframes and interpolation, choose a technique, move from storyboard to animatic, sync sound, export, and document the work.

sections.heading: Principles of movement
paragraphs: Animation creates the illusion of motion by showing slightly different images in quick sequence. The classic principles, described by Disney animators Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, help movement feel believable and appealing.

rows: A ball flattens on impact and stretches as it falls
Prepares the viewer for an action
Silhouette and camera angle focus attention
Straight ahead and pose to pose
Two ways to draw a sequence
Draw every frame in order, or key poses first
Parts keep moving after the main body stops
A ponytail swings after a character stops running
Motion speeds up and slows down naturally
A car accelerates from a stop
An arm swings in an arc
Number of frames sets speed and mood
Fewer frames feel fast and light

sections.heading: Timing, keyframes, and interpolation
paragraphs: Frame rate sets how many images appear per second. Film animation commonly uses 24 frames per second. Animating "on twos" means each drawing is held for two frames, so 12 drawings make one second; this is common in hand-drawn work. A 2-second action at 24 fps lasts 48 frames, which means 24 drawings on twos.

Keyframes mark the important poses or values at specific frames. In-betweens fill the frames between them. In digital tools, the software can calculate in-betweens, called tweening or interpolation. Linear interpolation moves at a constant speed and looks mechanical. Ease in and ease out slow the start and end. Bezier curves in a graph editor give precise control over acceleration.

example.scenario: A logo should slide in from the left over 1 second, pause for 2 seconds, then fade out over half a second, at 24 fps.
example.solution: Keyframe 1 at frame 0: logo off-screen left. Keyframe 2 at frame 24: logo centered, with ease out so it slows as it arrives. Keyframe 3 at frame 72: still centered at 100% opacity (2 seconds = 48 frames later). Keyframe 4 at frame 84: 0% opacity (half a second = 12 frames). Total length is 84 frames, or 3.5 seconds.

sections.heading: Choose a technique and tools

rows: Tactile, handmade look; needs steady camera and lighting
Realistic lighting and camera moves; steep learning curve
Text, shapes, and data in motion; great for explaining

paragraphs: Choose the technique that fits the story, the time available, and your skills. A short explanation of a process may work best as clean motion graphics; a character story may suit 2D. Hardware matters too: 3D rendering needs a capable computer and time, so plan render tests early.

sections.heading: From storyboard to export
steps: Concept: one-sentence idea and audience.
Script or outline, including any narration or dialogue.
Storyboard: panels for each scene with action, camera, and timing notes.
Animatic: the storyboard timed to the scratch audio, which shows pacing problems before animation begins.
Design: characters, backgrounds, and color palette; build assets.
Animation: block key poses, then refine timing and in-betweens.
Sound: record voice and effects, choose licensed or original music, and sync. For lip sync, match mouth shapes to sounds and place keyframes on audio peaks.
Render and export at the required settings, often MP4 (H.264) at 1920 x 1080, then watch the full file.
paragraphs: Keep a production record with dated drafts, the animatic, revision notes and reasons, the software and hardware used, and a source log with permissions for every asset and sound. In a presentation, show the final piece, then a few key drafts, and explain decisions using animation terms such as timing, easing, staging, and anticipation.

practice.task: Plan a 6-second bouncing-ball test at 24 fps with three bounces that get lower. How many frames is it? Name three principles you will show and where.
practice.answer: 6 x 24 = 144 frames. Principles: squash on each impact and stretch as the ball falls fast; slow in and slow out, with the ball slowing at the top of each arc and speeding up near the ground; arcs, with the ball's path curving between bounces. Timing shortens each bounce as height decreases, which shows the loss of energy.

terms.definition: A frame that defines an important pose or value in an animation.
Generating in-between frames between keyframes.
A storyboard edited to a timed soundtrack to test pacing.
Gradual acceleration and deceleration in motion.
Holding each drawing for two frames.

questions.prompt: A character crouches before jumping. This shows:
questions.explanation: Anticipation prepares the audience for the main action.

questions.prompt: A 3-second shot at 24 fps animated on twos needs how many drawings?
questions.explanation: 72 frames divided by 2 frames per drawing equals 36.

questions.prompt: Why make an animatic before animating?
choices: It tests timing and pacing cheaply
questions.explanation: Fixing timing in an animatic costs far less than redoing animation.

questions.prompt: Linear interpolation usually looks:
questions.explanation: Real motion accelerates and decelerates, so easing looks more natural.

questions.prompt: A ponytail that keeps swinging after a character stops shows:
questions.explanation: Loose parts continue moving after the main body stops.

modules.title: Prepared speech: research, structure, spoken style, and delivery
modules.summary: Research a topic, build a thesis and organization, write for the ear, revise for accuracy and audience, rehearse delivery within the rules, and review against the rating sheet.

sections.heading: Research and choose a thesis
paragraphs: Begin by reading the current topic carefully and listing what it asks. Brainstorm angles, then research the strongest with credible sources: studies, books, reputable news, and interviews. For a topic about leadership habits or service, look for specific, verifiable examples and research findings rather than general quotations. Record each fact with its source so you can cite it aloud.

A thesis is one sentence stating your main claim, such as "Curiosity is a skill we can practice, not a trait we are born with." This lesson uses that unrelated practice topic; students research and write their own competition speeches. Choose two or three main points that each support the thesis with evidence and examples.

sections.heading: Organize for listeners

rows: Curiosity at school, at work, in relationships
Problem: students stop asking questions; solution: three habits
Childhood questions, school years, adult careers
Why curiosity declines and what that costs

paragraphs: The introduction gets attention (a story, a surprising fact, or a question), states the thesis, and previews the points. Transitions signal movement: "That explains why curiosity matters. Now, how do we practice it?" The conclusion signals the end, summarizes the points, and closes with a memorable line that ties back to the opening.

sections.heading: Write for the ear and revise
paragraphs: A speech is not an essay read aloud. Use shorter sentences, everyday words, and repetition of key phrases so listeners can follow without rereading. Signposts ("first," "the second habit is") act as headings. Groups of three are easy to remember. Replace abstract claims with concrete examples and stories.

Cite sources orally: "According to a 2023 survey by the Pew Research Center..." Revise for accuracy (check every number and quotation), audience fit (would these judges understand every term?), and support (does every point have evidence?). Cut anything that does not serve the thesis. Read the draft aloud and mark where you stumble.

example.scenario: Revise this essay sentence for speaking: "Notwithstanding the prevalence of standardized curricula, the cultivation of inquisitiveness remains an underemphasized pedagogical objective."
example.solution: "Schools teach a lot of answers. They don't always teach us how to ask good questions." The revision splits one dense sentence into two short ones, uses everyday words, and creates a contrast listeners can hear.

sections.heading: Rehearse delivery within the rules
paragraphs: Most speakers talk at about 130 to 150 words per minute in a speech, so a 4-minute speech is roughly 520 to 600 words. Time several full rehearsals and adjust content, not speed. Check the current event rules for time limits, penalties, and whether notes are allowed; if allowed, use brief keyword notes, not a script.

Delivery includes vocal variety (rate, pitch, volume), purposeful pauses before key points, eye contact spread across the room, natural gestures that match your words, steady posture, and movement only with a purpose, such as stepping forward at a transition. Record yourself and watch for filler words and repeated habits. Rehearse in clothes and on a stage-like space if you can.

practice.task: Score a recorded rehearsal of your speech, or a 2-minute practice speech on "a skill worth practicing," using these criteria from 1 to 5: clear thesis, organized points with transitions, supporting evidence, vocal variety, eye contact, gestures, and timing. Write one specific change for your next rehearsal.
practice.answer: A useful self-review gives evidence for each score, such as "Transitions: 3; I moved from point one to point two with no signal at 1:10." The specific change is concrete and testable ("Add a one-sentence transition before each point and pause after it"), not general ("be more confident"). Compare the criteria with the event's actual rating sheet before the next rehearsal.

terms.definition: A one-sentence statement of a speech's main claim.
A word or phrase that tells listeners where the speech is going.
A persuasive pattern: attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, and action.
Changes in rate, pitch, and volume that add meaning and interest.
Naming a source aloud during a speech.

questions.prompt: About how many words fit a 5-minute speech?
questions.explanation: At 130 to 150 words per minute, five minutes is about 650 to 750 words.

questions.prompt: Which pattern ends with a call to action?
questions.explanation: Its final step is action.

questions.prompt: Writing for the ear means using:
choices: Short sentences and repetition of key ideas
questions.explanation: Listeners cannot reread, so clarity and repetition help.

questions.prompt: A speech runs 30 seconds long in rehearsal. The best fix is to:
questions.explanation: Rushing hurts clarity; trim material instead.

questions.prompt: Which is an oral citation?
questions.explanation: It names the source and date.

modules.title: Impromptu speaking: a preparation routine for unseen topics
modules.summary: Interpret a new prompt quickly, choose a theme and structure, gather examples, build a short outline, and deliver within the permitted time and materials.

sections.heading: A routine for the preparation time
paragraphs: Impromptu events give a topic and a short preparation period, then a speech of a few minutes. Check the current event guide for the exact preparation time, speaking time, and permitted materials, such as whether a note card is allowed. A fixed routine prevents panic, because you already know what to do with every minute.
steps: Read the prompt twice and underline the key words. Decide what it is really asking.
Choose one clear theme or answer in a single sentence. Take a position rather than listing every side.
Pick a structure from your memorized set.
Choose two or three examples: one personal, one from business or history, one from current events or a book you know well.
Plan an opening line and a closing line that echo each other.
Use any remaining time to rehearse the opening in your head.

sections.heading: Structures to memorize

rows: How it was, how it is, how it should be
What is wrong, why, what to do
One view, the other view, your conclusion

paragraphs: Practice each structure until you can outline a speech in under a minute. Keep a mental bank of 8 to 10 flexible examples: a personal challenge, a team experience, a well-known business turnaround, an inventor, a historical leader, and a recent local event. Most prompts can connect to several of them.

sections.heading: Annotated practice responses
paragraphs: Practice prompt: "Is failure a better teacher than success?" The outline below uses two sides, then a verdict.

example.scenario: Outline a 3-minute response to "Is failure a better teacher than success?"
steps: Opening: "The first time I ran a bake sale, we sold out in an hour, and I learned almost nothing. The second time, we lost money, and I learned everything." (A personal story that previews the theme.)
Thesis: "Failure teaches more, but only if we study it."
Side one: success shows what works, using a company that copied its own winning product line.
Side two: failure forces analysis, using the inventor who tested hundreds of materials before finding one that worked.
Verdict: failure teaches when we ask why; give two questions to ask after any setback.
Closing: return to the bake sale: "The money we lost that day was the cheapest business class I ever took."
example.solution: The outline works because it takes a clear position, uses different kinds of examples, and ends by echoing the opening story. Five or six key words on a note card are enough to deliver it.

sections.heading: Delivery from notes
paragraphs: Speak from key words, not sentences, and look at the audience, not the card. Use plain language; complex vocabulary under pressure leads to stumbles. Pause instead of saying "um." Use transitions to show structure aloud: "On the other hand," "That brings me to my verdict." Watch the time signals and finish the conclusion even if you must shorten a point.
Practice with new prompts several times a week, timing both preparation and delivery. Write your own prompts or trade them with a partner so they are truly unseen.

practice.task: Set a timer for your event's preparation time and outline a response to this prompt: "What makes a good team member?" Use PREP or three lessons, two different examples, and an opening that the closing echoes. Then deliver it aloud and time it.
practice.answer: A strong outline states one clear answer (for example, "A good team member makes others better"), uses two examples from different areas (such as a group project and a sports team), follows the chosen structure in order, and ends with a line that returns to the opening. During delivery, check whether you finished within the time, used transitions, and avoided reading from the card.

terms.definition: A speech delivered with little preparation on an unseen topic.
Point, reason, example, and point restated.
A set of prepared, flexible stories and facts that can fit many prompts.
A conclusion that returns to the speech's opening image or line.

questions.prompt: What is the first step after receiving an impromptu prompt?
choices: Read it carefully and decide what it asks
questions.explanation: Misreading the prompt leads to an off-topic speech.

questions.prompt: Which structure suits "How has technology changed communication?"
questions.explanation: Change over time fits a chronological structure.

questions.prompt: Notes for an impromptu speech should be:
choices: A few key words, if notes are permitted
questions.explanation: Key words keep you on track while maintaining eye contact.

questions.prompt: Why take a clear position instead of listing every side?
choices: It shortens the speech below the minimum
It gives the speech a coherent theme
questions.explanation: A single theme organizes the whole speech.

questions.prompt: If time is nearly up mid-point, you should:
choices: Shorten the point and deliver the conclusion
questions.explanation: A finished speech with a conclusion scores better than an unfinished one.

modules.title: Building a business presentation: research, recommendation, slides, and Q&A
modules.summary: Plan purpose and audience, use evidence without stereotypes, outline to a recommendation, design readable slides, rehearse with equipment, and handle questions as a team.

sections.heading: Purpose, audience, and evidence
paragraphs: Write one sentence stating what the audience should understand or do at the end. Business presentations usually lead to a recommendation, so research the problem, compare options, and choose one you can defend. Use credible evidence: research studies, government data, and named experts, with dates.

Topics about groups of people need extra care. For example, research on generations at work, such as Baby Boomers, Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z, often finds that differences within a generation are larger than average differences between generations, and that many differences reflect life stage rather than birth year. Strong presentations cite such evidence, avoid treating any group as all alike, and recommend practices that work for individuals, such as offering several communication channels, two-way mentoring, and clear expectations. Weak presentations repeat stereotypes. Students build their own competition presentation; the example below uses a different topic.

sections.heading: Outline to a recommendation
paragraphs: A reliable business outline is: opening (a hook and the question you will answer), background (the situation with key evidence), options (two or three, with criteria), recommendation (your choice and why), implementation (steps, people, timeline, cost), and closing (summary and call to action). Every slide or section should support the recommendation.

example.scenario: Annotated outline for an unrelated practice topic: "How should a 40-person company onboard remote employees?"
steps: Hook: "Half of our new hires this year never met a coworker in person during their first month." (Uses the company's own data to show the problem is real.)
Background: survey results on new-hire confusion and turnover, with source and date on the slide.
Options: (1) a self-paced online module, (2) a buddy program, (3) a one-week in-person start. Criteria: cost, speed to productivity, connection.
Recommendation: buddy program plus a short online module, because it scores best on connection at low cost. (Directly answers the question.)
Implementation: who trains buddies, a 30-60-90 day checklist, cost estimate, and how success is measured (90-day retention and a new-hire survey).
Close: "Approve a three-month pilot with the next six hires."
example.solution: Each annotation shows how the section earns points: evidence, comparison with criteria, a clear choice, a realistic plan, and a specific request.

sections.heading: Design slides that support you
paragraphs: Slides support the speaker; they are not the script. Use one main idea per slide, a headline that states the point ("Buddy programs cut first-month questions in half"), large readable fonts (generally 24 point or larger for body text), high contrast, and consistent layout. Show numbers as labeled charts with units and sources. Use accurate business vocabulary and define terms the audience may not know. Cite sources on the slide or in a final references slide.
Avoid paragraphs of text, decorative animations, and low-resolution images. Add speaker notes for your own reference if the rules allow them.

sections.heading: Rehearse, set up, and answer questions
paragraphs: Rehearse with a timer and the actual file on the type of equipment you will use. Bring the presentation in two formats (such as the native file and a PDF) and check the current rules on what equipment is provided and permitted. For teams, assign each section to a speaker, rehearse handoffs ("Now Jordan will walk you through the costs"), and make sure every member can answer questions on the whole presentation.

When answering questions, listen to the whole question, pause, answer directly in a sentence or two, then give one supporting reason. If you do not know, say so and explain how you would find out. Do not argue with a judge; acknowledge good points.

practice.task: Take a recommendation you could make to your school or chapter, such as a new club fundraising method. Write a six-part outline using the structure above, with at least one cited fact, two options and criteria, and a specific closing request.
practice.answer: A strong outline has a hook tied to a real problem, background with a named and dated source, two or three genuine options compared against stated criteria, one clear recommendation with reasons, an implementation plan with people, timeline, and cost, and a closing request that asks for a specific decision. It avoids slides that only list facts without leading to the recommendation.

terms.definition: The specific action a presentation asks the audience to approve or take.
The standards used to compare options, such as cost or speed.
A slide title that states the slide's main point as a sentence.
An oversimplified belief that all members of a group share a trait.

questions.prompt: Which slide title is most effective?
choices: New hires who had a buddy asked half as many questions
questions.explanation: A headline title states the point the evidence supports.

questions.prompt: Research on generations at work generally finds that:
choices: Every member of a generation behaves the same
Differences within generations are often larger than between them
Birth year determines all work values
questions.explanation: Individual and life-stage differences often outweigh generational averages.

questions.prompt: What is the best response to a question you cannot answer?
choices: Say so and explain how you would find out
questions.explanation: Honesty with a plan maintains credibility.

questions.prompt: Why bring the presentation in two formats?
choices: As a backup if one fails to open
questions.explanation: A backup format protects against software or equipment problems.

questions.prompt: Comparing options using stated criteria helps because it:
choices: Shows the recommendation is reasoned rather than arbitrary
questions.explanation: Criteria make the choice transparent and defensible.

modules.title: Designing and teaching a lesson: objectives, activities, and checks
modules.summary: Write measurable objectives, activate prior knowledge, sequence instruction with modeling and practice, plan access and timing, check understanding, teach live, and revise from evidence.

sections.heading: Write a measurable objective
paragraphs: A learning objective states what learners will be able to do by the end. The ABCD model includes the audience, the behavior (an observable verb), the condition, and the degree of success: "Given a monthly allowance and expense list (condition), seventh graders (audience) will build a balanced budget (behavior) with no math errors (degree)." Avoid verbs that cannot be observed, such as "understand" or "appreciate."

Bloom's revised taxonomy orders thinking from remember, understand, and apply to analyze, evaluate, and create. Match verbs to the level you intend: "list" is remembering; "compare" is analyzing; "design" is creating. A short lesson usually targets one main objective.

This lesson's examples use budgeting for middle school students. Competitors plan their own lesson on the assigned leadership topic, with content accurate and suitable for the assigned age group. Leadership skills such as communication, goal setting, teamwork, and responsibility can be taught the same way: define the skill, model it, practice it, and check it.

sections.heading: Plan the sequence
steps: Hook and prior knowledge (3 minutes): ask a question that connects to learners' lives, such as "What would you do with $50 a month?" A quick KWL (know, want to know, learned) chart surfaces what they already know and their misconceptions.
Direct instruction and modeling, "I do" (5 minutes): explain the idea briefly and think aloud through one example.
Guided practice, "we do" (7 minutes): solve a second example together, asking learners to suggest each step.
Independent practice, "you do" (8 minutes): learners complete a task alone or in pairs while the teacher circulates.
Check and close (5 minutes): an exit ticket question that directly measures the objective, then a summary.
paragraphs: List materials and their preparation, and time every part. Plan access needs using Universal Design for Learning: present information in more than one way (spoken, visual, written), offer more than one way to show learning, and build in choice and relevance to keep learners engaged. Plan for learners who finish early and for those who need extra support.

sections.heading: Check for understanding and handle misconceptions
paragraphs: Check understanding often, not only at the end. Quick checks include asking every learner to hold up a number of fingers for an answer, mini whiteboards, think-pair-share, and targeted questions with three to five seconds of wait time. Ask "why" follow-ups so you hear reasoning, not just answers.

Formative assessment happens during learning to guide teaching; summative assessment measures learning at the end. Anticipate common misconceptions and plan how to address them. In budgeting, students often treat savings as whatever is left over instead of a planned category; a contrasting example shows the difference.

example.scenario: During guided practice, half the class lists a phone bill as a "want."
example.solution: Pause and ask, "What happens if the phone bill isn't paid?" Discuss how needs and wants depend on the situation, then give a revised rule: a need is required for safety, health, school, or work obligations. Re-check with two new items before moving on. The teacher records this misconception to address earlier in the next version of the lesson.

sections.heading: Teach live and revise
paragraphs: In a live demonstration, judges may act as learners. Teach them as you would the intended age group: give clear directions, use the materials, ask real questions, and respond to their answers. Choose the section of the plan that best shows interaction, such as guided practice, rather than only lecturing. Keep to time and finish with a check that shows whether the objective was met.

After teaching, evaluate with evidence: what percentage of exit tickets met the objective, which mistakes repeated, and which activity took longer than planned. Revise the plan accordingly and note what changed. Score your plan against the event's lesson-plan rating criteria before submitting.

practice.task: Write an ABCD objective, a 20-minute sequence with times, and one exit ticket question for an unrelated topic: teaching fifth graders to write a polite email request.
practice.answer: Sample objective: "Given a scenario (condition), fifth graders (audience) will write an email request (behavior) that includes a greeting, a clear request, a reason, and a thank-you (degree)." Sequence: hook, 2 min ("Which email would you answer first?" comparing two examples); model, 4 min; guided practice, 5 min writing one together; independent practice, 7 min; exit ticket and close, 2 min. Exit ticket: "Write a two-sentence email asking your librarian to renew a book, with a greeting and a thank-you." It directly measures the objective.
