modules.title: Business plan research, operations, and supporting sections
modules.summary: Research the industry, market, and competitors with checked evidence, plan operations, legal structure, staffing, and advisers, and assemble milestones, risks, and appendices in the required sequence.

sections.heading: Industry, market, and competitor research
paragraphs: A business plan persuades a reader that the idea is sound, so every claim needs evidence. Industry research describes the industry's size, growth, trends, and regulations, using sources such as the Census Bureau's business data, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the SBA, trade associations, and reputable news. Record each fact with its source and date.

Market research defines the target customer and estimates demand. Total addressable market (TAM) is everyone who could buy the product; serviceable available market (SAM) is the part the business can reach; serviceable obtainable market (SOM) is the realistic share it can win. Build estimates from the bottom up when possible: number of likely customers times purchases per year times price. Support assumptions with primary research such as surveys, interviews, or a small test.

Competitor analysis compares direct competitors (same product), indirect competitors (different product, same need), and substitutes. A comparison table of price, quality, location, service, and weaknesses shows the gap the business will fill. Conclude each research section with what it means for the business, not only what the data says.

example.scenario: A fictional phone repair kiosk in a mall estimates its market from the bottom up.
steps: The county has about 120,000 smartphone owners within a 15-minute drive (from population data and a published ownership rate).
Assume 10% need a repair each year: 12,000 repairs (cite the source of the rate, or label it an assumption tested by a survey).
Three competitors already serve the area. Assume the kiosk can win 8% of repairs in year one: 960 repairs, or about 80 a month.
At an average price of $80, year-one revenue is about $76,800.
example.solution: Each step is traceable to a source or a labeled assumption, so a reader can check it. The financial model then uses 80 repairs a month as its steady-state volume, which keeps the research and the numbers consistent.

sections.heading: Operations, legal structure, and people
paragraphs: The operations section explains how the business will work day to day: location and layout, equipment, suppliers, production or service process, quality control, hours, and technology. State realistic constraints, such as lease terms, supplier lead times, or how many repairs one technician can complete in a day.

Explain the chosen legal structure and why it fits, plus required licenses, permits, insurance, and intellectual property protection. Staffing covers the roles needed, when each will be hired, pay, and how the owner's time is used. Compensation should match local wage data. Advisers, such as an accountant, attorney, mentor, or board, strengthen a plan when their roles are specific.

sections.heading: Growth, risks, milestones, and appendices
paragraphs: Long-term development explains how the business will grow: new locations, products, or channels, and what must be true first. A risk section names the main risks (lower demand, a new competitor, a key supplier failing, the owner's illness) and the plan for each. Milestones give dates and measures: opening day, break-even month, second technician hired.

Supporting documents, such as resumes, quotes from suppliers, a lease summary, survey results, and detailed financial statements, go in appendices referenced in the text. Follow the event's required report sequence, section names, page limits, and formatting. A plan that is strong but out of order or over the limit can lose points.

sections.heading: Submission and presentation checks
steps: Compare the table of contents with the current guide's required sections, in order.
Count pages exactly as the guide defines them, including or excluding the title page and appendices as stated.
Check that every number in the text matches the financial statements.
Open the exported PDF on another device and confirm fonts, charts, and links.
Prepare a presentation that follows the plan's logic and the rating sheet: opportunity, solution, market evidence, operations, financials, and the request.
Practice answers to likely questions: "How did you estimate demand?" "What if sales are 20% lower?" "Why this location?"
paragraphs: The captured Maryland guide for Business Plan contains an older school year in one instruction. Confirm the current wording with the official guide or adviser before relying on season-specific details.

practice.task: For a business idea of your own, write a three-row competitor table (competitor, price, strength, weakness) and one sentence stating the gap your business fills. Then name one risk and its response.
practice.answer: A strong table includes at least one indirect competitor or substitute, uses checked prices with dates, and lists real weaknesses rather than assumed ones. The gap sentence connects directly to those weaknesses (for example, "No competitor offers same-day repair within the mall"). The risk is specific and the response is practical, such as a second supplier for a key part.

modules.title: Building a linked financial model for a startup
modules.summary: Turn assumptions into startup costs, a sales forecast, monthly cash flow, break-even, and linked financial statements, then test what happens when assumptions change.

sections.heading: Start with an assumptions sheet
paragraphs: A financial model is only as good as its assumptions. Put every assumption on one sheet with its source: prices, costs per unit, volumes, wages, rent, loan terms, and growth rates. Every other sheet should calculate from these cells, so changing one assumption updates the whole model. Never type a number into a formula that should come from an assumption.

Continuing the fictional phone repair kiosk: the average repair price is $80. Parts average 35% of price ($28) and card fees are 3% ($2.40), so variable cost is $30.40 and contribution margin is $49.60 per repair. Monthly fixed costs are rent $1,500, wages $2,400, insurance $150, software $60, and marketing $290, totaling $4,400.

rows: Cash reserve (3 months of fixed costs)

sections.heading: Break-even and funding
paragraphs: Break-even volume is fixed costs divided by contribution margin: 4,400 / 49.60 = 88.7, so the kiosk needs about 89 repairs a month to cover costs before loan payments. That is above the 80-repair steady state from the market research, which is an important finding: the plan must raise volume, raise prices, or cut fixed costs.

Funding covers startup costs. Suppose the owner invests $10,000 and borrows $18,200 through a microloan at 8% for 5 years. The monthly payment is $369.03. In the first month, interest is 18,200 x 0.08 / 12 = $121.33 and the rest, $247.70, repays principal. Interest goes on the income statement; principal repayment does not, but both reduce cash.

sections.heading: Forecast monthly cash flow
paragraphs: New businesses usually ramp up. Assume 60 repairs in month 1, then 10 more each month. The table shows the first three months.
bullets: The three months use $3,891 of the $13,200 reserve, so the reserve is adequate for the ramp-up if the forecast holds.
Depreciation on the $10,000 of tools and build-out, about $167 a month over 5 years, reduces profit on the income statement but not cash.
The statements link: net income flows to owner's equity on the balance sheet; ending cash on the cash flow statement equals cash on the balance sheet; loan principal repaid lowers the loan liability.

sections.heading: Test the assumptions
paragraphs: Sensitivity analysis changes one assumption at a time to see what matters most. If price rises to $90 with the same costs, variable cost becomes $34.20 (35% parts plus 3% fees), contribution is $55.80, and break-even falls to 4,400 / 55.80 = about 79 repairs. If volume is 20% below forecast, the reserve lasts fewer months. Present a base case, a conservative case, and an optimistic case, and explain which assumptions drive the difference.

Common errors include mixing monthly and yearly figures, forgetting owner pay, ignoring seasonality, counting loan proceeds as revenue, and forecasting growth with no evidence. Check that the balance sheet balances in every period.

example.scenario: A judge asks, "What happens if a competitor cuts prices and you must charge $70?"
example.solution: At $70, variable cost is $26.60 (35% plus 3%), contribution is $43.40, and break-even rises to 4,400 / 43.40 = about 102 repairs a month. The kiosk would need more volume, a cheaper parts supplier, or lower fixed costs. A presenter who has run this scenario can answer in seconds.

practice.task: Using the kiosk model, calculate break-even if rent rises to $1,800 (fixed costs $4,700) and the price stays $80. Then calculate monthly profit before loan payments at 100 repairs.
practice.answer: Break-even: 4,700 / 49.60 = 94.8, so about 95 repairs. Profit at 100 repairs: 100 x 49.60 - 4,700 = 4,960 - 4,700 = $260 a month before the $369 loan payment, which means cash flow is still negative by about $109 a month. The plan needs a higher price or volume of about 103 repairs, since (4,700 + 369) / 49.60 = 102.2, to cover the loan.

terms.definition: An estimated input to a model, such as price or volume, stated with its basis.
One-time costs to open a business, plus any initial cash reserve.
Testing how results change when one assumption changes.
Money set aside to cover losses while a business ramps up.

modules.title: Chapter reports: community service and annual business report evidence
modules.summary: Assess community needs, keep participation records with accurate percentages, evaluate outcomes, document publicity and permissions, connect activities to the Program of Work, and assemble the report and presentation.

sections.heading: Confirm the rules first
paragraphs: The Community Service Project and the Local Chapter Annual Business Report are chapter events judged on a written report and a presentation. Their captured Maryland guides include dates from earlier seasons, so confirm the eligible activity period, school year, required sections, page limits, and categories with the current official guide and your adviser before writing season-specific instructions. Keep the confirmed rules in a checklist at the front of your working file.
Both reports reward the same habit: every claim in the report is backed by a record. Start keeping records at the first meeting, not the week before submission.

sections.heading: Choose and justify a community project
paragraphs: A needs assessment finds what the community actually needs. Sources include partner organizations, local data, surveys, and interviews with people affected. Baseline evidence describes the situation before the project, such as the number of families on a food pantry's waiting list. Partner input matters: a shelter may need hygiene kits more than canned food. Document why you chose one project over others, using criteria such as need, chapter capacity, and measurable impact.

sections.heading: Track participation accurately
paragraphs: Keep sign-in records for every activity with member names, roles, and hours. Count unique members, not total sign-ins: a member who attends five events is one participating member. The participation percentage equals unique participating members divided by total chapter membership.

example.scenario: A chapter has 64 members. Sign-in sheets from eight events show 142 total sign-ins by 41 different members, totaling 356 volunteer hours.
steps: Unique participation: 41 / 64 = 64.1% of members.
Average events per participating member: 142 / 41 = 3.5.
Average hours per participating member: 356 / 41 = 8.7.
example.solution: Report 64.1% participation, not 142 / 64 = 222%, which counts the same people repeatedly. Keep the sign-in sheets so a judge's question can be answered with records.

sections.heading: Evaluate outcomes, publicity, and permissions
paragraphs: Outputs are what the chapter did, such as 600 hygiene kits assembled. Outcomes are what changed because of it, such as a shelter that could give a kit to every new resident for four months. Collect feedback from partners and participants, compare results with the baseline, and write recommendations for next year based on what worked and what did not.

Document publicity with copies of articles, social posts with reach figures, flyers, and announcements, each dated. Get written permission before using photos of people, especially minors and people served by the project, and protect their privacy. Credit sources and partners accurately.

sections.heading: Connect the chapter year to the Program of Work
paragraphs: A Program of Work is the chapter's annual plan: goals, the activities that serve each goal, the person responsible, target dates, and how success will be measured. The annual business report shows how the year's activities carried out that plan. Organize evidence by the report categories in the current guide, which typically include areas such as career preparation, community service, partnerships, fundraising, publicity, and participation in state and national programs.

Include required elements such as the chapter president's remarks, written truthfully by the president. Use a consistent sequence, a table of contents, page numbers, and appendices for supporting documents, and count pages exactly as the guide defines them. In the presentation, walk through the year chronologically or by goal, showing how activities connected to goals and what the results were.

rows: Resume workshop with a local HR manager

Across all three, 58 different members took part. (a) What is the chapter's overall participation rate? (b) Why can't you add the three event counts?
practice.answer: (a) 58 / 80 = 72.5%. (b) Adding 35 + 42 + 50 = 127 counts members who attended more than one event several times, which overstates participation. Unique members must be counted from the combined records.

modules.title: Event planning from first plan to final report
modules.summary: Plan purpose, audience, schedule, owners, venue, and vendors; budget forecasts against actuals; manage layout, permits, safety, and backups; run the day with records; and report results honestly.

sections.heading: Plan the event
paragraphs: Begin with the purpose and measurable goals: "Host a family financial literacy night for 120 attendees that raises $1,000 for the chapter's scholarship fund." Define the audience, then build a backward timeline from the event date with every task, its owner, and its due date. Hold short planning meetings with an agenda and recorded action items.

Choose a venue using criteria such as capacity, location, accessibility, cost, parking, equipment, and availability of backup dates. Get written quotes from vendors (catering, audiovisual, rentals), compare at least two, and read contracts for deposits, cancellation terms, insurance requirements, and what happens in bad weather. Some details, such as permits, insurance, and food rules, depend on the venue and local government, so record what you must verify and with whom.

sections.heading: Budget forecasts and actuals
paragraphs: A budget lists expected income (tickets, sponsorships, donations) and expenses. In-kind support, such as donated food or a free venue, should be listed separately at its fair value so readers see the event's true cost without inflating cash. Include a contingency of about 10% for surprises. After the event, record actual figures and calculate the variance for each line.

rows: In-kind: venue donated by school (fair value)

bullets: Explain each large variance: attendance fell short because of a schedule conflict, but an added sponsor covered the gap.
Keep every receipt and deposit record; the report's cost claims should match them.

sections.heading: Layout, staffing, safety, and backups
paragraphs: Draw a floor plan showing entrances, registration, seating, stations, accessible routes, and emergency exits, and stay within the venue's posted capacity. Assign staff and volunteers to roles with a shift schedule and a briefing sheet. Plan safety: first aid, emergency contacts, a lost-child procedure for family events, and food allergy labeling. Write backup plans for likely problems such as rain, a speaker canceling, technology failure, or low attendance.

sections.heading: Promote, run the day, and report
paragraphs: Promotion follows the audience: flyers through schools, social posts, partner newsletters, and personal invitations, each with a tracking method such as a registration source question. On the event day, use a run sheet with times and owners, track attendance with sign-in or ticket scans, keep an incident log, and record any unexpected problem and how it was solved.

Collect feedback with a short survey (three to five questions, including one open question). The final report and presentation show evidence of execution (photos with permission, attendance records), attendee satisfaction results, financial results against the budget, what went well, what went wrong, and specific improvements for next time.

example.scenario: Thirty minutes before the event, the projector fails.
example.solution: The tech lead switches to the backup plan: the presentation loaded on a second laptop connected to the gym's TV cart, plus printed handouts of key slides. The incident log records the time, the problem, the response, and a lesson: test the venue projector the day before. Reporting this honestly shows judges real problem-solving.

practice.task: Forecast: 200 tickets at $8 and $300 of sponsorships; expenses of $600 for food and $250 for supplies. Actual: 176 tickets, $450 of sponsorships, food $540, supplies $270. Calculate forecast net, actual net, and the variance, and write one sentence explaining it.
practice.answer: Forecast net: 1,600 + 300 - 600 - 250 = $1,050. Actual net: 1,408 + 450 - 540 - 270 = $1,048. Variance: $2 unfavorable. Explanation: ticket income was $192 below forecast, but an extra $150 of sponsorship and $60 of food savings nearly offset it, while supplies ran $20 over.

modules.title: A complete data investigation: question, cleaning, analysis, visuals, and recommendations
modules.summary: Frame a question, check and document a dataset, clean it reproducibly, analyze with fair comparisons and uncertainty, build three clear visuals, and recommend feasible actions.

sections.heading: Frame the question and check the source
paragraphs: A good analysis question is specific, answerable with available data, and tied to a decision: "Which branch library programs reach the most residents per 1,000 people, and where should next year's program budget go?" This lesson uses a fictional library dataset; students choose their own data for the competition topic.

Check every source: who published the data, how it was collected, what period it covers, how each field is defined, and its known limitations. Prefer official and documented sources. Save the original file unchanged, and record the download date and URL.
Write a data dictionary listing each column's name, meaning, type (number, text, date), units, and allowed values. It catches problems early, such as a column mixing counts and percentages.

sections.heading: Clean and transform reproducibly
steps: Copy the raw file; never edit the original.
Remove exact duplicate rows and record how many were removed.
Standardize categories, such as "N. Branch," "North," and "north branch" all becoming "North."
Handle missing values deliberately: leave them blank and exclude them, fill them using a stated rule, or drop rows, and record the choice and count.
Check outliers: a program with 9,000 attendees at a 40-seat room is probably an entry error. Verify it before removing or correcting it.
Create calculated fields, such as attendance per 1,000 residents or percent change.
Keep a cleaning log, or a script in Python or R, so someone else can repeat every step and get the same result.
paragraphs: A spreadsheet works for small datasets if each step is documented. A short script is more reproducible, because the steps are the code.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.read_csv("library_programs_raw.csv")
df = raw.drop_duplicates()
df["branch"] = df["branch"].str.strip().str.title().replace({"N. Branch": "North"})
print("Missing attendance:", df["attendance"].isna().sum())
df = df.dropna(subset=["attendance"])
df["per_1000"] = df["attendance"] / df["residents"] * 1000
df.to_csv("library_programs_clean.csv", index=False)

sections.heading: Analyze fairly and state uncertainty
paragraphs: Compare like with like. Raw counts favor large groups; rates adjust for size. Branch A had 4,800 program visits and serves 24,000 residents; Branch B had 3,000 visits and serves 10,000 residents. A has more visits, but B reaches 300 per 1,000 residents compared with A's 200, so B's programs reach a larger share of its community.
Describe the uncertainty. Small samples vary a lot; a 50% jump from 4 to 6 attendees means little. Survey results have margins of error. Data from one year may reflect an unusual event.

Correlation is not causation. If branches with more programs have more visitors, the programs may cause visits, busier branches may schedule more programs, or both may depend on a third factor such as location near a school. To support a causal claim, you need a comparison that rules out other explanations, such as the same branch before and after a change, with other conditions steady.

sections.heading: Visualize and recommend
paragraphs: Choose the chart for the question: bar charts compare categories, line charts show change over time, scatter plots show relationships between two numbers, and tables give exact values. Start bar chart axes at zero, label axes with units, use a clear title that states the finding, add a source note, and avoid 3D effects and pie charts with many slices. Make sure colors are distinguishable for people with color vision deficiency.

Recommendations follow from findings: each states the action, the evidence, the resources needed (money, staff, time), feasibility, how success will be measured, and possible social or economic effects, including on groups who might be left out.

example.scenario: Three visuals for the library analysis.
steps: Bar chart: "Branch B reaches the most residents per 1,000," program visits per 1,000 residents by branch, axis from zero, source note.
Line chart: "Weekend programs grew while weekday programs stayed flat," monthly attendance by program time over two years.
Scatter plot: "Branches near schools draw more youth attendance," distance to nearest school versus youth attendance per 1,000, with a note that this shows association, not proof of cause.
example.solution: Recommendation: shift 15% of next year's program budget to weekend sessions at Branches A and C, measured by visits per 1,000 residents in a six-month pilot. Resources: existing staff with adjusted schedules. Limitation: one year of data; repeat the analysis after the pilot.

practice.task: A dataset shows Store X had 1,200 complaints and Store Y had 300. Store X served 400,000 customers; Store Y served 50,000. (a) Compare complaint rates per 1,000 customers. (b) Write one sentence a careful analyst would add before recommending action.
practice.answer: (a) X: 1,200 / 400,000 x 1,000 = 3.0 per 1,000. Y: 300 / 50,000 x 1,000 = 6.0 per 1,000. Y's rate is twice X's despite fewer complaints. (b) Sample sentence: "Before acting, check whether both stores record complaints the same way and whether this pattern holds across several months."

sections.heading: Report the process
paragraphs: A process report or presentation explains the question, data sources and their limits, cleaning steps and counts, methods, findings with visuals, recommendations, and limitations, in that order. Judges should be able to repeat the analysis from your files. Map each section to the rating criteria so every scored requirement is easy to find.

A count adjusted for size, such as visits per 1,000 residents.
A third factor that affects both variables being compared.
A value far from the others that may be an error or a real extreme.

modules.title: Supply chain plans: brief analysis, sourcing, costs, and demand
modules.summary: List every brief requirement, select suppliers ethically, model landed and fulfillment costs, forecast demand with early signals, plan capacity, and link choices to the rating criteria.

sections.heading: Analyze the brief first
paragraphs: The captured Supply Chain Management guide's topic title and detailed planning text appear inconsistent. Confirm the current brief with the official source or adviser before building a topic-specific solution, and keep both versions noted until it is resolved.

Turn the brief into a requirement list: the product, customers and region, service commitments (delivery time, cost to the customer, returns), any donation or sustainability commitments, budget limits, and required report sections. Each later decision should point back to a requirement. This lesson uses a fictional company selling refillable cleaning kits, which is unrelated to the competition topic.

sections.heading: Source ethically and choose suppliers
paragraphs: Supplier selection compares cost, quality, reliability, capacity, lead time, location, financial stability, and ethical practices such as fair labor and environmental standards. A weighted scorecard makes the comparison transparent. Request audits or certifications, ask about subcontractors, and avoid relying on a single supplier for a critical part.

Production planning sets what to make and when. Make-to-stock builds inventory ahead of demand; make-to-order builds after orders arrive. Packaging must protect the product, fit carrier size limits, meet labeling rules, and match sustainability commitments. Distribution choices range from one national warehouse (lower inventory, longer delivery) to several regional centers (faster delivery, more inventory and cost).

sections.heading: Model costs and profit per order
paragraphs: Landed cost is the full cost of getting a unit to your warehouse: purchase price plus freight, duties, insurance, and handling. Fulfillment cost is the cost of getting an order to the customer: picking and packing labor, packaging, and shipping. Contribution per order is the price minus landed cost and fulfillment cost. Donation commitments, such as 5% of each sale, are another variable cost per order.

example.scenario: A cleaning kit costs $6.00 from the supplier, plus $0.80 freight, $0.30 duty, and $0.10 insurance per unit. Fulfillment costs $1.50 labor, $0.90 packaging, and $4.20 shipping per order. The kit sells for $24, and the company donates 5% of the price.
steps: Fulfillment cost: 1.50 + 0.90 + 4.20 = $6.60.
Donation: 24 x 5% = $1.20.
Contribution per order: 24.00 - 7.20 - 6.60 - 1.20 = $9.00.
example.solution: Each order contributes $9.00 toward fixed costs. Shipping is the largest single cost after the product, so distribution decisions strongly affect profit. Show this breakdown in the plan so judges see where each choice changes cost.

sections.heading: Forecast demand and plan capacity
paragraphs: Forecasting methods include the moving average (average of recent periods), the weighted moving average (more weight on recent periods), and exponential smoothing (new forecast = old forecast + alpha x (actual - old forecast)). With monthly demand of 400, 460, and 520, a three-month average forecasts 460; weights of 0.5, 0.3, and 0.2 (newest first) forecast 0.5 x 520 + 0.3 x 460 + 0.2 x 400 = 478.

New products have no history, so use early signals: preorders, waitlist sign-ups, test-market sales, and similar products' launches. Limited releases create urgency but risk stockouts. Plan capacity responses before they are needed: safety stock, overtime, a second shift, a backup contract manufacturer, or pausing preorders. State what triggers each response, such as preorders exceeding 1,000 units.

practice.task: Using exponential smoothing with alpha = 0.3, last month's forecast was 450 units and actual demand was 520. (a) Forecast next month. (b) If each order now costs $0.60 more to ship, what is the new contribution per order in the example above?
practice.answer: (a) 450 + 0.3 x (520 - 450) = 450 + 21 = 471 units. (b) Fulfillment rises to $7.20, so contribution falls to 24.00 - 7.20 - 7.20 - 1.20 = $8.40 per order.

sections.heading: Link the plan to the rating criteria
paragraphs: Organize the final plan so each rating criterion has a clear section: the brief analysis, sourcing and supplier choice, production and packaging, distribution, the cost model, the demand forecast and capacity plan, risks, and how the plan meets service and sustainability commitments. Use consistent assumptions across every section, and present a base case and a stress case such as demand 30% above forecast or a supplier delay of two weeks.

modules.title: Supply chain operations: purchasing, warehousing, inventory, and transportation
modules.summary: Compare purchasing methods, receive and store goods, pick and fulfill orders, calculate EOQ and reorder points, measure order cycle time, choose transport modes, and handle returns.

sections.heading: Purchasing and supplier relationships
paragraphs: Purchasing buys the materials and services the business needs at the right quality, quantity, time, and price. Methods include spot buying for one-time needs, blanket purchase orders that set terms for repeated purchases over a period, competitive bidding through requests for quotation (RFQ) or proposals (RFP), and e-procurement systems. Centralized purchasing gains volume discounts; decentralized purchasing responds faster to local needs.

Good purchasing raises productivity: reliable, on-time supplies keep production running, and quality materials reduce rework. Collaboration tools include shared forecasts and vendor-managed inventory, where the supplier monitors and refills the buyer's stock. Records include the purchase order, receiving report, invoice, and supplier performance data.

sections.heading: Receive, store, pick, and ship
steps: Receiving: check quantities and condition against the purchase order and packing slip; record discrepancies.
Put-away: store items in assigned locations recorded in the warehouse system.

Picking: discrete picking fills one order at a time; batch picking collects items for several orders at once; zone picking assigns workers to areas; wave picking releases groups of orders at scheduled times.
Packing: choose the right box and packing material, include the packing slip, and label correctly.
Shipping: select the carrier, generate tracking, and confirm pickup.
Inventory update: the system records every movement so stock counts stay accurate.
paragraphs: Warehouses can be private (owned by the company), public (rented space), or distribution centers built for fast movement. Cross-docking moves goods from incoming trucks straight to outgoing trucks with little or no storage. Order cycle time is the time from order placement to delivery; reducing any step, such as order processing, picking, or transit, shortens it.

sections.heading: Inventory calculations
paragraphs: The economic order quantity (EOQ) balances ordering costs against holding costs: EOQ = square root of (2 x annual demand x cost per order / holding cost per unit per year). The reorder point tells when to order: daily demand x lead time in days, plus safety stock. ABC analysis classifies items by value: A items are the few that make up most of the inventory value and get the closest control.

example.scenario: A distributor sells 12,000 units a year. Each order costs $50 to place, and holding one unit for a year costs $3. Daily demand is 40 units, lead time is 5 days, and safety stock is 60 units.
steps: EOQ: square root of (2 x 12,000 x 50 / 3) = square root of 400,000 = about 632 units.
Orders per year: 12,000 / 632 = about 19.
Reorder point: 40 x 5 + 60 = 260 units.
example.solution: Order about 632 units whenever stock falls to 260. The safety stock covers demand spikes or delays during the 5-day lead time.

sections.heading: Transportation and reverse logistics

rows: Higher cost per ton over long distances
Low cost for heavy, bulky goods over land
Fixed routes; needs trucks for the last leg
Lowest cost for large volumes, global trade
Most expensive; weight and size limits
Continuous flow of liquids and gas
Containers move between ship, rail, and truck

paragraphs: Choose modes by product value, weight, urgency, distance, and cost. Assess carriers on on-time percentage, damage rate, cost per unit, and tracking. Global shipments add customs documents, Incoterms, and longer lead times.

Reverse logistics handles returns and end-of-life products: authorize the return, receive and inspect, then restock, refurbish, recycle, or dispose. Fast, clear returns improve customer loyalty and recover value. Distribution must follow laws such as hazardous materials shipping rules and driver hours-of-service limits, and ethical practice includes fair labor and honest delivery promises. Current trends include automation, nearshoring, real-time tracking, and lower-emission transport. Risks include single-source suppliers, port disruptions, and weather, managed with backup suppliers, safety stock, and contingency routes.

practice.task: Annual demand is 7,200 units, ordering cost is $40, and holding cost is $4 per unit per year. Daily demand is 30 units, lead time is 6 days, and safety stock is 45. Calculate EOQ and the reorder point, then choose a transport mode for urgent replacement parts worth $2,000 each shipped across the country.
practice.answer: EOQ: square root of (2 x 7,200 x 40 / 4) = square root of 144,000 = about 379 units. Reorder point: 30 x 6 + 45 = 225 units. Air freight fits the urgent, high-value, lightweight parts, since speed matters more than cost per unit.
